What clauses and Long Phrases as Subject
When you use a what , that, or who clause as the subject of a sentence, you have shifted the emphasis away from the words that sit in the subject position.

Look at these examples:
Original Sentence
The type is the first thing we need to choose.
(the emphasis here is on ‘type' because it's in the subject position)

Noun Clause Sentence
What we need to choose first is the type.
(the emphasis is now on ‘what we need to choose' as it has been moved to the subject position)
So, if you want to place emphasis on the verb, direct object, or another part of the sentence, you use a what-phrase (or sometimes a that-clause).

For example:
He really wanted to emphasize his experience.
      becomes
What he really wanted to emphasize was his experience.
This is how we form “What” clauses.

Writing a résumé can be a daunting experience, especially if you have never written one. There are certain rules that can be applied when it comes to organizing one. Not all résumés are the same, but here are some important sections that employers in a variety of industries will expect to see.

a. Header
Here you write your name in bold and in a font that is slightly larger than the rest of the résumé.
Make sure you include your contact information (i.e. mailing address, phone number, and e-mail).

b. Objective Statement
Although this is optional, employers expect to see a statement showing the direction you want to go. You can also include your work preferences.

c. Education
Here you add any information regarding your degree. Include where and when you graduated. You may include your GPA if it is strong.

d. Experience
Use either a chronological and combination formats. Make sure you add any relevant experience. For example include jobs, internships, volunteer experiences and coursework.

e. References
Finally, make sure you include a reference section at the end of your résumé. Simply indicate that your references are “available upon request”. Bear in mind that you should have at least three people who can serve as your references.
Example: We need to look at the sections of your résumé.

Adam: What's next?
Kristi: What I think we should do next is look at the sections of your résumé. What I don't understand is why you only have your contact information, your experience, and your hobbies.
Adam: I thought this would suffice.
Kristi: Adam, what you want your résumé to be is eye-catching. There are certain sections that employers will expect to see.
Adam: Like what?
Kristi: I'd recommend adding a job objective statement.
Adam: Okay. What do I write about?

Kristi: What employers expect to see is a statement showing the direction you want to go. You can also include your work preferences.
Adam: Can I include skills I bring to the position? I could add some of those action verbs you mentioned.
Kristi: Absolutely. Another section you want to include is your education. In this section, you could add any information regarding your degree. Don't forget to include where and when you graduated.
Adam: Should I include my GPA?
Kristi: Only if it is an asset. If you feel your GPA isn't strong, make sure you put more of your non-academic experience with an emphasis on your strengths and skills.
Adam: Got it.
Kristi: I've also noticed you only listed your formal job experience.

Adam: I know. But those are the places where I gained all my prior experience.
Kristi: What about volunteer experience or unpaid experience? You could have them here as well.
Adam: I volunteered as a content editor for two university publications.
Kristi: Then, what I'd suggest is listing them here. Finally, make sure you include a reference section at the end of your résumé.
Adam: Should I write their names and contact information as well?
Kristi: No, simply indicate that your references are “available upon request”. Bear in mind that you should have at least three people who can serve as your references.
Adam: Gotcha! Thanks, Kristi!
